q: A start-up runs a customer relationship management product it licenses from a vendor. The vendor patches the platform; the start-up decides who gets accounts and what data is entered. After a data leak caused by a former employee's still-active account, who holds primary responsibility for that failure?
opts: The vendor, because it operates the entire software stack
Neither party, since the account belonged to an individual rather than an organization
The start-up, because user access and data handling stay with the customer in SaaS
Shared equally, because SaaS removes the distinction between the parties
why: In SaaS the provider manages the application and below, but customers remain responsible for identity lifecycle, access settings and the data they enter. A stale account is a customer joiner-mover-leaver failure. The vendor's operation of the stack does not extend to deprovisioning the customer's staff, and responsibility is split by layer, not evenly.

q: A team moves a batch-processing application from servers it manages to a managed container platform where the provider operates the host operating system and orchestration. Compared with IaaS, which responsibility has MOST clearly shifted to the provider?
opts: Writing and testing the application's authentication logic
Classification and protection of the sensitive data that the application stores and processes on the platform
Defining which staff may deploy new application versions
Patching and hardening of the host operating system and orchestration layer
why: Managed platforms move the lower layers (host OS, runtime, orchestration) to the provider. Data classification, application logic and deployment authorization remain with the customer at every service model, which is why they are tempting but wrong.

q: A regional hospital group, a university and a public health agency jointly fund one cloud environment built to a common research-compliance standard and open only to those organizations. Which deployment model is this?
opts: Hybrid cloud, because several organizations contribute infrastructure
Private cloud, because access is restricted to named organizations
Community cloud, because the participants have the same regulatory needs
Multi-cloud, because multiple customers participate
why: A community cloud is shared by organizations with a common concern, here the same compliance standard. Private cloud serves one organization. Hybrid joins different deployment models, and multi-cloud means several providers; neither is described.

q: An architect is asked why a workload that scales out automatically at peak and releases servers overnight is described as elastic rather than merely scalable. What is the BEST answer?
opts: Capacity is added and removed automatically in response to demand
Resources are shared among tenants to cut cost
The provider guarantees a contractual availability percentage for the service each month
The application can run on larger instance types if needed
why: Elasticity is automatic provisioning and release matching demand. A larger instance is vertical scaling by hand, availability guarantees are an SLA matter, and sharing is resource pooling or multi-tenancy.

q: Which statement about the cloud service broker role is MOST accurate?
opts: A broker adds value but the customer stays accountable for its own data and compliance
A broker is the independent party that certifies provider controls
A broker replaces the need for a contract with the underlying provider
A broker takes on full legal liability for every item of data that is processed through its platform
why: Brokers intermediate, aggregate or add value to services, but accountability for data and compliance cannot be outsourced. Independent certification is the auditor's role, and liability and contracts still need explicit treatment.

q: A security architect must keep the contents of a financial model confidential even from the cloud provider's administrators while the model is being computed on a rented virtual machine. Which technology addresses this requirement BEST?
opts: Full-disk encryption with a provider-managed key
TLS 1.3 between the client and the virtual machine
Tokenization of the model's output files
Confidential computing using a hardware-based trusted execution environment
why: Confidential computing protects data in use by processing it inside an encrypted, isolated hardware enclave. Disk encryption covers data at rest and, with provider-held keys, does not exclude the provider. TLS covers data in transit, and tokenizing outputs does nothing for the computation itself.

q: A company wants the freedom to move a critical application to another provider within a few weeks if prices rise. Which design choice BEST supports that goal?
opts: Replicate all data to an on-premises server that only IT staff may access
Adopt each provider's proprietary managed database services wherever they improve performance
Build on open standards and containers, keep data portable and document an exit plan
Negotiate a three-year price lock with the incumbent provider
why: Portability comes from open standards, portable formats and tested exit procedures. Proprietary services deepen lock-in, a price lock does not create a way out, and a private copy of the data does not make the application portable.

q: Which architectural principle BEST reflects the move from perimeter-based protection to cloud-native security?
opts: Allow unrestricted traffic between workloads in the same virtual network
Verify every request using identity, device and context, not network location
Place all workloads inside a single private subnet and rely on its boundary to limit exposure
Rely on the provider's physical security for logical access control
why: Zero trust treats identity and context as the control point because there is no trusted network edge in cloud. Flat internal trust and a single subnet recreate the perimeter fallacy, and physical security does not replace logical access control.

q: A team stores purchase records on a managed distributed ledger and later receives a lawful erasure request from a customer. What is the MOST significant design problem this reveals?
opts: Ledgers require the provider to hold every participant's private key in order to validate entries
Ledgers cannot be replicated across regions, so a regional outage loses the whole record
Ledgers cannot be encrypted when the data is at rest, so every stored purchase record is exposed
Immutable ledger entries cannot be removed, which conflicts with deletion obligations for personal data
why: Immutability is a feature for integrity and a defect for erasure rights, so personal data should stay off-chain with only references or hashes on it. Ledgers can be encrypted and replicated, and participants keep their own keys.

q: Why should an organization start planning its move to post-quantum cryptography today for data that must remain confidential for twenty years?
opts: Quantum computers will make all symmetric hashing completely unusable as soon as they exist
Adversaries can collect encrypted traffic now and decrypt it once quantum capability exists
Quantum computing can erase data from encrypted storage remotely
Cloud providers will stop supporting current TLS versions this year
why: Harvest-now, decrypt-later makes long-lived secrets vulnerable well before capable quantum computers arrive, motivating crypto agility and migration planning. The other statements overstate or invent effects.

q: A customer asks which document tells them how much downtime the provider will tolerate before credits are owed. Which is the BEST answer?
opts: The shared responsibility matrix
The service level agreement
The provider's SOC 2 report
The data processing addendum
why: The SLA states measurable service targets and remedies. A SOC 2 report describes controls, the responsibility matrix divides security duties, and a data processing addendum covers personal data handling.

q: An IoT fleet sends telemetry to a cloud ingestion service. Which design decision MOST reduces the risk of a stolen device injecting false data?
opts: Use a shared API key embedded in the firmware of all devices
Accept data from any source address in the manufacturer's range
Encrypt telemetry with a single key that is stored in each device's clear-text configuration file
Give each device a unique certificate-based identity and authenticate every connection
why: Per-device identities allow revocation of one compromised unit without disrupting the fleet. A shared key is exposed by one extracted device, IP ranges are spoofable and a clear-text key offers no protection.

q: Which activity is MOST clearly the cloud customer's responsibility regardless of the service model?
opts: Deciding who may access their data and how it is classified
Maintaining the hypervisor and host firmware
Replacing failed disks in the provider's storage arrays
Controlling physical access to the provider's data centers
why: Data governance and access decisions always rest with the customer. Hypervisors, data-center access and hardware maintenance are provider duties in all service models.

q: An architect reviews a design against ISO/IEC 17789 cross-cutting aspects and finds no plan for leaving the provider. Which aspect has been overlooked?
opts: Maintenance and versioning
Reversibility
Availability
Performance
why: Reversibility concerns retrieving customer assets and having remaining copies deleted on exit. Availability, maintenance and versioning, and performance are separate aspects and do not address exit.

q: A data science team wants to fine-tune a hosted foundation model with customer support transcripts. Under shared responsibility, which duty stays with the customer?
opts: Classifying and protecting the training data and access to the tuned model
Operating the provider's model-serving network
Securing the physical GPU servers that run the training job
Patching the underlying operating system of the managed training service's hosts
why: Even on a fully managed AI service, the training data, access to the resulting model and the choice of what to feed it belong to the customer. Hardware, platform patching and provider networking are provider duties.

q: Which TWO characteristics distinguish a true cloud service from ordinary hosted infrastructure? (Choose two.)
opts: The customer owns the physical servers
Workloads cannot move between regions
Customers can provision resources on demand without human interaction
Usage is metered so it can be measured and billed
Capacity is fixed in a multi-year contract
why: On-demand self-service and measured service are NIST essential characteristics. Fixed capacity contracts and customer-owned hardware are traits of traditional hosting, and cloud workloads commonly can move between regions.

q: Which TWO statements about multi-cloud strategies are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: They guarantee workload portability without any code change
They can reduce dependence on one provider and improve resilience
They remove the need for a shared responsibility analysis
They are identical to hybrid cloud by definition
They increase the work needed for consistent identity, logging and policy
why: Using several providers spreads risk but multiplies operational and governance complexity. Each provider still needs a responsibility analysis, portability is never automatic and hybrid cloud is a different concept.

q: Which THREE items are properly the provider's responsibility in an IaaS deployment? (Choose three.)
opts: Guest operating system patching
Hypervisor and host patching
Availability of the underlying storage service
Physical data-center security
Firewall rules for customer virtual networks
why: Facilities, hypervisor and core service availability belong to the provider. In IaaS the customer patches guest operating systems and configures their own network controls.

q: Which TWO technologies are most directly aimed at limiting exposure of data while it is being processed? (Choose two.)
opts: Full-disk encryption
Transport Layer Security
Confidential computing with trusted execution environments
Homomorphic or secure multi-party computation techniques
Hash-based message authentication
why: Both enclaves and privacy-preserving computation protect data in use. TLS and disk encryption cover transit and rest, and message authentication provides integrity of messages rather than confidentiality of processing.

q: Which TWO risks are especially associated with edge computing deployments? (Choose two.)
opts: Inability to use encryption on any link
Many physically accessible nodes that attackers can tamper with
Complete reliance on a single central data center
Inconsistent patching across a widely distributed fleet
why: Edge widens the physical and patching surface. It reduces dependence on one center and can use encryption normally.

q: In a SaaS model the customer is relieved of all accountability for data protection because the provider operates the application.
opts: True
False
why: The provider operates the application stack, but the customer remains accountable for its data, user access and configuration choices.

q: A hybrid cloud always involves two or more different cloud providers.
opts: True
False
why: Hybrid means distinct deployment models, typically private and public, bound together. Two public providers is multi-cloud.

q: Measured service means the provider monitors resource use so it can be reported, controlled and billed.
opts: True
False
why: Metering underlies pay-per-use billing, quotas and cost anomaly detection.

q: Multi-tenancy is a risk the customer can eliminate by choosing any reputable provider.
opts: True
False
why: It is inherent to pooled cloud resources; customers manage the risk through isolation choices, encryption and dedicated options, not by eliminating it.

q: The CCSP outline expects candidates to consider how related technologies such as containers, serverless functions, edge computing and AI affect cloud architecture and security.
opts: True
False
why: The outline asks you to consider how containers, edge, confidential computing, AI and similar technologies affect architecture and security.

q: Reversibility means the customer can retrieve their data and have the provider delete the remaining copies when the relationship ends.
opts: True
False
why: It is one of the cross-cutting aspects and should be backed by contract terms and verified deletion.

q: Moving a workload from IaaS to PaaS leaves the customer's responsibilities exactly unchanged.
opts: True
False
why: Operating system and runtime duties move to the provider; application, identity and data duties remain.

q: Data in use can be protected using trusted execution environments built into the processor.
opts: True
False
why: Hardware enclaves isolate and encrypt memory during computation, which is the aim of confidential computing.

q: A university wants its agency partners to resell a managed analytics service under their own brand, adding billing and support. The partners contract with the provider but the university's student data flows through the platform. Which statement about accountability is MOST accurate?
opts: Accountability is split evenly among the university, the reseller and the provider because each handles the data
The reseller becomes the legal owner of the data once it adds billing and support
The university remains accountable to regulators for the student data, whatever the reseller adds
Accountability passes to the provider once the reseller contract is signed, because the agency only resells the service
why: Brokers and resellers add value or convenience but do not take over the data owner's regulatory accountability. Ownership does not move by reselling, the provider is a processor or custodian rather than the accountable owner, and an even split is not how accountability works.

q: A security architect reviews a proposed design and asks, for each activity in the reference architecture, which role performs it, so that every control has an owner. What is the PRIMARY benefit of this exercise?
opts: It exposes controls that nobody owns before the service goes live
It removes the need for a written contract, because the activity mapping already records each duty
It proves the provider holds a current ISO certificate
It allows the customer to hand the operation of every control to the provider and stop reviewing them
why: Mapping activities to roles is a responsibility checklist: a control with no owner is a gap. It does not transfer duties to the provider, does not evidence certification and does not replace a contract.

q: A company is comparing two designs. Design one uses compute instances the company patches. Design two uses a managed function service where the company supplies only code. Which statement BEST compares the responsibility for operating system patching?
opts: In the first design the provider patches the guest operating system because it owns the hardware
Both designs leave host patching to the customer, because compute services are always customer-managed in every model
In the second design the provider patches the host, while the company still owns function permissions and code
Neither design requires any patching by the company, because cloud resources are kept secure by the provider by default
why: Serverless pushes host operating system patching to the provider; the customer keeps permissions, code, dependencies and data. In the first design the guest operating system is the customer's job, and cloud does not remove patching.

q: A consultant reviews a company's cloud risk register and notes that most of the 'top threats' it lists concern misconfiguration, weak identity controls and insecure APIs rather than provider breaches. Which conclusion follows MOST directly?
opts: Encryption of all stored data would remove the listed risks entirely, so no other control needs attention
The provider's hypervisor is the most likely entry point for attackers
Moving to a private cloud eliminates these threat categories, because the listed threats occur only in public clouds
Governance, change control and identity management on the customer side deserve the most attention
why: Industry threat reports consistently rank misconfiguration, identity and API weaknesses at the top, which are customer-side concerns managed through change control and access governance. The hypervisor is rarely the entry point, encryption does not fix misconfiguration and private clouds still have configuration and identity risk.

q: A customer retired an encrypted volume by destroying its key and must now give an auditor assurance that the data is unrecoverable. Which evidence is MOST convincing?
opts: Key management records proving every copy of the key was destroyed, including backups and escrow
A console screenshot showing the volume with a deleted status and a timestamp
The provider's marketing statement that deleted customer data is always unrecoverable
A report showing that the guest operating system overwrote the volume once before release
why: Cryptographic erasure is only as strong as the key destruction, so the convincing evidence is the key lifecycle record and proof that no copy survives in backups or escrow. A console status shows only logical deletion, a marketing claim cannot be verified, and a guest-level overwrite may not reach replicas or wear-leveled blocks.

q: A multinational wants to ensure engineers can only create resources in two approved regions to honor data residency promises. Which control MOST directly enforces this?
opts: Encryption of all data with provider-managed keys, which hides content from outsiders but not from the platform
An alert that reports resources in other regions after a week
Training engineers on the residency policy at onboarding and trusting them to follow it for each deployment
A policy that denies resource creation outside the approved regions at the account level
why: A preventive guardrail enforced centrally blocks the violation; training and delayed alerts only detect or hope, and provider-managed encryption does not constrain location.

q: A finance director asks whether to buy a new intrusion detection subscription. Expected annual loss from the targeted threat is 80000 and the control would cut it to 30000 for an annual cost of 20000. What is the BEST conclusion?
opts: Approve it, because the annual loss reduction exceeds its annual cost
Defer it, because a control must remove the whole risk to be worthwhile
Reject it, because the residual annual loss is still above zero
Reject it, because the control costs more than the remaining loss
why: The reduction of 50000 exceeds the 20000 cost, so the safeguard has positive value. Perfect risk removal is not required, and the cost is compared with the avoided loss, not with the residual loss.

q: Two cloud providers both offer an acceptable SLA. The architect wants a first-pass evaluation that is objective rather than based on presentations. What should she do FIRST?
opts: Ask each provider to submit its own ranking of its strengths and choose the highest self-score
Select the cheaper option and review security after migration
Choose the provider with the larger market share, since popularity indicates that its controls have been proven
Define the security and compliance criteria, then compare each provider's evidence against them
why: Evaluation starts with criteria derived from business and regulatory requirements; evidence such as audit reports and certifications is then compared. Market share, self-ranking and post-migration review do not verify requirements.

q: A procurement team notes that a provider's hypervisor holds a Common Criteria certification at a high assurance level. How should the architect interpret this?
opts: It replaces the need for a SOC 2 report on the service, because both assess the same scope and criteria
It confirms that the provider meets every privacy regulation applicable to the customer's workloads
It proves every customer workload on the platform is secure
It evaluates that product against a stated security target and does not certify the entire cloud service
why: Common Criteria evaluates products against a security target, so it supports one component's assurance. It cannot vouch for customer workloads, replace service-level audit reports or establish privacy compliance.

q: A cloud customer requires that cryptographic keys be generated in validated hardware. A vendor presents a certificate for a FIPS 140-2 validated module that was issued in 2019. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
opts: Confirm the exact module and version are validated, check its status and plan for FIPS 140-3
Accept it as sufficient, because FIPS 140 validation applies to a provider as a whole organization
Reject it outright, because FIPS 140 applies only to software libraries and never to hardware modules
Ignore the date because validation never changes
why: Validation is specific to a module, version and operating environment, and 140-2 modules moved to the Historical list in September 2026 (usable only in existing systems), so replacement under 140-3 should be planned. FIPS 140 covers hardware and software modules, not whole providers, and status does change.

q: A security team deploys a machine learning model that scores sign-in events and automatically blocks accounts above a threshold. Which risk deserves the MOST attention before enabling automatic blocking?
opts: Machine learning cannot analyze identity logs because they contain too little structured information
Automated blocking decisions are prohibited in every jurisdiction, so the model can only report
False positives locking out legitimate users when the model is not validated against real traffic
The model cannot be hosted in a cloud environment because training data must stay on premises
why: Unvalidated models cause false positives and false negatives; consequential actions need testing, tuning and human review. Models can run in the cloud, can analyze identity logs and are not generally prohibited.

q: A bank trains a fraud model using transaction data pulled from a partner's shared storage. An analyst notices that some records look unusual and cannot say where they came from. Which control would have BEST reduced the risk of poisoned training data?
opts: Moving training to a larger compute instance so poisoned records are diluted by the extra capacity
Increasing the number of training epochs so that the model averages out any bad records
Verifying data provenance and integrity before the data enters the training pipeline
Encrypting the finished model at rest, which protects the file but not the data it learned from
why: Provenance and integrity checks catch tampered or untrusted data at the entry point. More training, encrypting the output and bigger instances do nothing about bad inputs.

q: An organization plans a customer-facing system that uses a high-risk automated decision about loan eligibility. Which activity is MOST consistent with responsible AI governance?
opts: Rely on the provider's published marketing claims of fairness instead of testing outputs for the use case
Remove all logging to protect customer privacy
Keep the model logic secret from internal risk and compliance teams to protect intellectual property
Assess bias and impact, document the model's purpose and keep human oversight of decisions
why: Impact and bias assessment, documentation and human oversight are core to ethical and regulatory expectations such as the EU AI Act's high-risk duties. Secrecy from risk teams, removing logs and trusting marketing undermine accountability.

q: Which TWO statements about the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: The NIST framework is a binding law with fines for non-compliance
The EU AI Act classifies AI systems into risk tiers with stricter duties for higher risk
The EU AI Act applies only to organizations established in the United States
Both documents prohibit the use of cloud platforms for AI
The NIST framework organizes AI risk work into govern, map, measure and manage
why: The NIST framework is voluntary guidance with four functions. The EU AI Act is a regulation with a risk-based structure that can reach providers and deployers outside the EU when systems are used there. Neither bans cloud use.

q: Which TWO design measures best support ephemeral computing without losing investigative ability? (Choose two.)
opts: Disabling logging to reduce cost
Shipping logs to a protected central store before instances terminate
Storing evidence on the instance's local disk
Automating snapshot capture of a suspect instance before it is replaced
Allowing administrators to patch instances manually in place
why: Short-lived resources disappear with their local state, so evidence has to leave first through central logging and automated capture. Manual in-place changes defeat immutability, local disks vanish and disabled logs leave nothing to investigate.

q: Which THREE items are valid inputs when evaluating a cloud service provider against criteria? (Choose three.)
opts: Data location, key management and exit terms in the contract
The provider's incident history and breach transparency
The number of followers the provider has on social media
A competitor's opinion of the provider
Independent audit reports and certifications with their scope statements
why: Evaluation depends on verifiable evidence: scoped audit reports, contract terms and incident record. Popularity and competitor opinions are unverified.

q: The ISO/IEC 17788 cloud service partner role includes sub-roles such as the service developer, auditor and service broker.
opts: True
False
why: Partners support either customer or provider; the outline lists customer, provider, partner, broker and regulator as the roles to know.

q: A Common Criteria certificate for a product proves that a cloud service built on it meets every customer requirement.
opts: True
False
why: It evaluates the product against its security target only, not a whole service or a customer's workload.

q: FIPS 140-2 validated modules remain acceptable for new federal systems without limit, because FIPS 140-3 is optional.
opts: True
False
why: FIPS 140-3 supersedes 140-2, and after September 21, 2026 modules validated only under 140-2 are on the Historical list for existing systems.

q: The outline expects a CCSP to weigh ethical concerns and regulatory requirements when comparing AI and machine learning options.
opts: True
False
why: AI and ML appear in the outline in cloud design, data protection and operations, including ethics, validation of data sources and regulation.

q: Geofencing by IP geolocation is a complete control for data residency because it cannot be bypassed.
opts: True
False
why: Geolocation can be spoofed or routed around; combine regional policies, identity controls and encryption.

q: An attacker who gains rights in the orchestration layer of a cloud platform could create, change and delete large numbers of workloads in one operation. Which control BEST protects this building block?
opts: Larger virtual machine sizes so the orchestrator has spare capacity during attacks
Additional storage replicas in a second region so that deleted workloads can be rebuilt
Column-level encryption of every database that the orchestrated workloads can reach
Strong authentication, least privilege, approvals and full logging on orchestration and management calls
why: Orchestration acts with broad privilege, so access to it needs the tightest identity controls and auditing. Database encryption, replicas and capacity do not stop a malicious operation from being issued.

q: A provider lets customers upload their own code and runs it on a managed runtime while operating the servers and operating system. Under the ISO/IEC 17788 capability types, what does the customer receive?
opts: Platform capabilities, because customers deploy and run their own code on the provider's runtime
Infrastructure capabilities, because customers provision and manage the virtual machines themselves
None of the three, because managed runtimes fall outside the capability model entirely
Application capabilities, because the provider supplies the finished software that customers merely use
why: Deploying customer code on a provider-managed runtime is a platform capability. Infrastructure capabilities leave the operating system to the customer, and application capabilities mean using the provider's own software.

q: A product team wants a new managed service to be safe without customers having to tune it: minimal exposed functionality, restrictive settings and secure behavior out of the box. Which design approach describes this?
opts: Shift-right testing that finds weaknesses only after customers report them
Secure by design and secure by default
Defense by compliance checklist completed shortly before general availability
Security through obscurity combined with a detailed configuration hardening guide
why: Secure by design builds protection into the architecture and secure by default ships with safe settings, so the customer does not carry the burden. A hardening guide pushes the work to customers, and late testing or checklists add little.

q: A DevOps team releases many times a day, yet security reviews happen only before quarterly milestones and have become a backlog. What is the BEST way to keep security in step with delivery?
opts: Defer security work until after release and fix issues only when customers report them
Move all security staff into a separate gate team that approves every individual change by hand
Build automated security checks into the pipeline and share ownership of findings with developers
Cut the release frequency to the number of reviews the security team can handle each quarter
why: DevSecOps brings checks to where changes happen, such as scanning and policy gates, so feedback is fast and scales. Throttling releases, manual gates and post-release fixing do not scale or are too late.

q: A security team's machine learning model flags unusual network behavior. After the company migrates many workloads to a new architecture, the model begins missing attacks. What is the MOST likely cause and response?
opts: Model drift on the new traffic patterns, so validate against current data and retrain
A flaw in the cloud provider's hypervisor, so open a ticket with the provider and wait for a platform patch to be released
Normal behavior, since models never need review once they pass their first validation
Excess encryption of network flows, so disable TLS to restore full visibility to the model
why: A model trained on old traffic degrades when behavior changes; monitoring performance and retraining on validated, representative data restores it. Disabling TLS and waiting for a patch address nothing, and models need ongoing review.

q: A hiring tool built on a cloud machine learning service ranks candidates, and an audit finds consistently lower scores for one protected group. Which response BEST addresses the ethical concern?
opts: Hide the demographic fields from the audit report so the ranking appears neutral to reviewers and the regulator
Rely on the cloud provider's SOC 2 report as evidence that the model outputs are fair
Examine the training data for bias, test fairness, document the results and add human oversight
Keep the model but encrypt the scoring results so that candidates cannot question them
why: Bias usually comes from data and features, so the fix is analysis, fairness testing, documentation and human review. Hiding fields, citing an infrastructure report or encrypting results leaves the harm in place.

q: A security orchestration playbook automatically disables any account that triggers a high-severity alert. Analysts fear false positives will lock out executives and critical service accounts. Which design is BEST?
opts: Tier the response: automate low-impact actions, add approval for high-impact accounts
Exempt all privileged accounts from every alert so the playbook can never cause an outage
Remove automation entirely, since SOAR tools should only ever produce reports for analysts
Keep full automation and ask affected executives to open a ticket if they are locked out
why: Risk-based tiers keep the speed of automation while limiting the blast radius of an incorrect action. Removing automation loses the benefit, exempting privileged accounts opens the biggest hole, and ignoring false positives harms the business.

q: Using a managed AI service removes the customer's need to assess regulatory requirements that apply to how the AI output is used.
opts: True
False
why: The customer remains accountable for lawful use, such as high-risk classifications under the EU AI Act, whichever party runs the model.

q: A cloud customer must prove to an auditor that a decommissioned database is unrecoverable, but cannot access the provider's physical disks. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Ask the provider to confirm it will degauss the disks eventually
Move the database to another region and delete the first copy
Overwrite the logical volume once with zeros before releasing it
Encrypt the data with customer-controlled keys and destroy all copies of the keys
why: Cryptographic erasure is the accepted cloud answer because customers cannot physically sanitize shared media. A single logical overwrite may not touch all replicas, a promise to degauss is unverifiable and moving regions just leaves more copies.

q: A company learns that its object storage contains several unknown buckets with customer records. What should the security architect do FIRST to bring the data under control?
opts: Deploy DLP policies that block all uploads to cloud storage
Run data discovery to find and inventory where sensitive data is stored
Ask the data custodian to delete all unknown buckets
Apply the strictest encryption setting to every bucket in the account immediately
why: You cannot classify, encrypt or govern data you have not located; discovery comes first. Blanket encryption and blocking are premature, and deleting unknown buckets risks destroying data under legal hold or business need.

q: A law firm sends a confidential contract to an external party and must be able to revoke that party's access after the project ends, even if the file has been downloaded. Which control BEST meets this requirement?
opts: Transport Layer Security on the file transfer
Full-disk encryption on the sender's laptop
Data loss prevention rules on the outbound email gateway and web proxy
Information rights management applied to the document
why: IRM is persistent protection that follows the file and can be revoked. DLP only gates egress, TLS protects the transfer in transit and disk encryption protects one device.

q: A developer wants realistic customer data in a test environment, but the test team does not need real identities. Which approach MOST reduces risk?
opts: Apply irreversible static masking before copying data to the test environment
Encrypt the production copy with the same key as production
Tokenize the data and share the vault with the test team
Copy production data into the test environment and restrict access to the test team only
why: Irreversible masking removes real values so a test breach exposes nothing. Restricting access still leaves real data in a weaker environment, sharing the token vault defeats the point and reusing the production key enlarges exposure.

q: Under privacy law, which statement about pseudonymized data is MOST accurate?
opts: It no longer requires a lawful basis for processing
It is anonymous and falls outside privacy regulation
It remains personal data because the separate mapping allows re-identification
It can be freely shared with any third party
why: Pseudonymization is a safeguard, not an exemption: if re-identification is possible with additional information, the data is still regulated. Only effective anonymization removes it from scope.

q: A regulation requires records to be kept for seven years, yet a pending lawsuit concerns some of those records. A lifecycle rule would delete anything older than three years. What should the architect do?
opts: Let the three-year rule run and restore from backups if needed
Delete the records to reduce eDiscovery exposure
Suspend deletion for the affected records under a legal hold and align the retention rule to the longest applicable requirement
Move the records to a cheaper storage tier and keep the existing three-year deletion rule running unchanged
why: Legal and regulatory retention outrank convenient lifecycle rules; a legal hold must prevent destruction. Deleting relevant records can be spoliation, relying on backups is unreliable and tiering does not stop deletion.

q: Who is accountable for deciding the classification of a dataset hosted in a public cloud?
opts: The cloud provider's security team
The database administrator who runs the service
The cloud service broker
The data owner within the customer organization
why: The owner determines classification and access; custodians and providers implement. Accountability for data is never transferred through custody or brokerage.

q: A bank wants to stop employees from uploading files containing account numbers to personal cloud storage, including over encrypted connections. Which solution is MOST suitable?
opts: Encrypting every file with a shared team password
A firewall rule blocking all outbound traffic on port 443 for every employee workstation
A cloud access security broker or DLP control that can inspect the content
A policy memo reminding staff of acceptable use
why: Content-aware DLP at a point that can decrypt or see activity addresses the requirement. Blocking port 443 breaks the business, a shared password is weak and does not prevent upload, and a memo is not a technical control.

q: A data science team is building a model from several public and internal sources. Which data security concern is MOST specific to this scenario?
opts: The model's training job runs inside a private virtual network with restricted egress
The dataset is stored as compressed files
The team uses a notebook to explore the data
Poisoned or tampered training data silently degrading the model's integrity
why: Integrity and provenance of training data are the particular risk, since poisoned inputs corrupt every resulting model. Network placement, compression and notebooks are ordinary engineering choices without the same specific risk.

q: In most cloud scenarios involving personal data, how are the customer and provider classified?
opts: Both as joint data subjects
Provider as data owner and customer as custodian
Customer as processor and provider as controller
Customer as controller and provider as processor
why: The customer decides purposes and means and so is controller; the provider processes on its instructions. The reverse is wrong unless the provider uses the data for its own purposes.

q: Why does erasure coding across several locations improve a cloud storage system's durability?
opts: Data is split into fragments with redundancy so lost fragments can be rebuilt
The provider mirrors all data into the customer's data center
Data is encrypted using a different key for each fragment
Every copy of the data is stored in full in every region that the provider operates worldwide
why: Dispersion with redundancy lets the system reconstruct data after partial loss. Full copies everywhere is replication, per-fragment keys are unrelated and mirroring to the customer is not how it works.

q: A security team can see a sudden volume of queries from a privileged database administrator reading many customer rows at night. Which control would have given the BEST independent evidence of this activity?
opts: A stricter password and rotation policy for all database administrators
Encryption of the database volume
Database activity monitoring feeding a separate log store
Daily snapshots of the database
why: Independent monitoring of queries records and can alert on privileged abuse. Volume encryption does not stop an authorized session reading data, passwords do not log activity and snapshots capture state, not reads.

q: Which TWO activities belong to the earliest phases of the cloud data life cycle? (Choose two.)
opts: Legal hold release
Moving to long-term archival storage
Classifying the data when it is created
Verified destruction of media
Assigning an owner and applying initial labels
why: Classification and ownership are applied when data is created. Destruction, archiving and hold release occur later in the cycle.

q: Which TWO measures MOST effectively reduce the risk of public exposure of cloud object storage? (Choose two.)
opts: Disabling versioning on every bucket
Account-level controls that block public access by default
Naming buckets with hard-to-guess names
Relying on the bucket's default network location
Continuous posture monitoring that alerts on public or unencrypted buckets
why: Preventive guardrails and detective posture monitoring address misconfiguration. Obscure names are security by obscurity, defaults are the common cause of exposure and versioning is a recovery feature unrelated to exposure.

q: Which TWO statements about data classification are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Handling rules such as encryption and access follow from the label
It applies only to structured data
It is assigned by the cloud provider after migration
It is unnecessary if data is encrypted
It must be reviewed because sensitivity can change over time
why: Labels drive controls and need periodic review. Providers do not decide the owner's classification, encryption does not replace classification and it applies to all data types.

q: Deleting a file in the cloud console guarantees that every replica of the underlying data has been physically destroyed.
opts: True
False
why: Logical deletion does not guarantee physical erasure; customers rely on cryptographic erasure and provider attestations.

q: Data discovery should generally take place before classification and DLP rules are tuned.
opts: True
False
why: You must know where data is and what it contains before labeling it or writing effective prevention rules.

q: Anonymized data that cannot reasonably be re-identified is generally outside the scope of privacy regulations such as GDPR.
opts: True
False
why: Properly anonymized data no longer relates to an identifiable person, unlike pseudonymized data.

q: Information rights management can restrict printing and forwarding of a document after it has been shared.
opts: True
False
why: IRM policies are embedded and enforced when the document is opened, and access can be revoked.

q: A cloud customer can transfer accountability for data protection to the provider by signing a processor contract.
opts: True
False
why: A contract assigns processing duties, but the controller stays accountable to regulators and data subjects.

q: Static data masking creates a copy with realistic substitute values that cannot be reversed to the original.
opts: True
False
why: Static masking is typically irreversible and suits non-production copies.

q: A regulator requires that the cloud provider must never be able to decrypt a firm's trading records. Which key strategy BEST satisfies this requirement?
opts: Provider-managed keys held in the provider's HSM
Provider-managed keys held in the provider's HSM with rotation every 90 days
Bring your own key imported into the provider's KMS
Hold your own key in an on-premises HSM outside the provider's control
why: HYOK keeps key material outside the provider so it cannot decrypt. BYOK still imports the key where the provider's service can use it, and provider-managed keys, however rotated or hardened, are provider-accessible.

q: A company wants to retain the ability to revoke access to data at any time by deleting key material, but accepts that the provider's service performs encryption and decryption. Which option fits?
opts: Hashing the data with a salted algorithm
Customer-managed keys in the provider's key service, with customer-controlled policies
Provider-managed keys with default settings
Storing the key beside the encrypted data in the same account to make recovery easier
why: Customer-managed keys let the customer disable or delete the key and so cut off access. Defaults leave control to the provider, hashing is irreversible and cannot protect data that must be read, and co-locating the key with data undermines separation.

q: In envelope encryption, what is the main advantage of wrapping each data encryption key with a key encryption key?
opts: Rotating or revoking one key encryption key controls many data keys without re-encrypting data
It removes the need for any key management service
It makes the encryption algorithm quantum resistant
It lets the provider decrypt the data on demand without needing any customer approval or key policy check
why: The KEK protects DEKs, so rotation and revocation happen at the KEK level. Envelope encryption still needs key management, does not change algorithm strength and does not give the provider extra decryption rights.

q: An e-commerce site wants to shrink the part of its environment that must meet card-data compliance rules. Which technique MOST directly achieves this?
opts: Tokenization so most systems only hold surrogate values
Encrypting card numbers with a key stored in the application
Compressing card numbers before storing them
Hashing card numbers with an unsalted algorithm
why: Systems that hold only tokens are generally out of scope for the real value, shrinking compliance effort. Unsalted hashes of low-entropy numbers are easily reversed, compression is not security and an application-held key leaves the data in scope.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes tokenization from encryption?
opts: A token is created by applying a block cipher and a secret key to the original value
A token can be reversed by anyone holding the public key
A token has no mathematical relationship to the value, which sits in a vault
A token is always shorter than the original value
why: Tokens are random surrogates mapped in a vault, so there is nothing to decrypt. Reversal by public key, size and cipher-based creation describe encryption or format-preserving encryption instead.

q: A team stores API keys for a payment service in the configuration file of a container image. What is the BEST remediation?
opts: Encrypt the configuration file using a hard-coded password
Move the keys into a secrets manager and inject them at runtime with rotation enabled
Rename the keys so they are harder to recognize
Restrict the container registry to internal users only
why: A secrets manager provides access control, audit and rotation, and keeps secrets out of images. A hard-coded password just moves the secret, registry restrictions do not remove embedded secrets and renaming is obscurity.

q: Which situation BEST justifies using a hardware security module rather than software-only key storage?
opts: The team wants to avoid learning key management
A policy requires tamper-resistant, validated protection of root keys
The application needs much faster bulk encryption of large video files at low cost
The data is classified as public
why: HSMs provide tamper-resistant custody and validated modules for sensitive keys. They are not for speeding bulk encryption, do not eliminate key management duties and public data does not justify the cost.

q: Two parties who have never met need to exchange a symmetric session key over an untrusted network. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Hash the key with SHA-256 and send the hash
Send the symmetric key in an email protected by a long and complex subject line
Use a pre-shared key printed on the license agreement
Use asymmetric cryptography or a key agreement protocol to establish the key
why: Asymmetric methods or key agreement solve the key distribution problem. Email is plaintext, a hash of a key does not convey it and a printed shared secret cannot be rotated or scaled.

q: An architect's design relies on encrypting data with a key kept in the same storage account as the data. What is the PRIMARY weakness?
opts: Reading the key from the same account makes the encryption run too slowly to be usable
Anyone who gains access to the account can obtain both data and key, defeating the encryption
Regulations prohibit storing cryptographic keys in any cloud storage service at all
Encrypted data cannot be backed up or replicated while its key sits in the same account
why: Key separation is a basic principle: compromise of the account should not hand over both parts. Keys can be stored in cloud services, backups work fine and performance is not the issue.

q: A company discovers its TLS certificate expired and a customer-facing service went down. Which practice would MOST directly prevent a recurrence?
opts: Replace TLS with a proprietary encryption protocol maintained by the application team
Automate certificate issuance and renewal and monitor expiry dates
Disable certificate validation in clients
Issue certificates with ten-year lifetimes
why: Automation and monitoring address the lifecycle failure. Long lifetimes increase exposure when keys are compromised, disabling validation removes authentication and proprietary protocols are riskier.

q: A firm must plan for the day current public-key algorithms are no longer safe. Which design principle is MOST useful?
opts: Crypto agility, so algorithms can be swapped without re-architecting
Encrypting data twice with the same algorithm
Standardizing every system on the longest public-key length that is available today
Moving all keys to a single central server
why: Agility lets teams migrate to new algorithms. Longer keys of a vulnerable family do not help against quantum attacks, double encryption with one algorithm shares the weakness and one central server is a single point of failure.

q: Which TWO statements about BYOK are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: The provider can never access the key in any form
BYOK and HYOK are the same thing
The customer generates the key material and imports it into the provider's key service
The provider's service can still use the key to decrypt data on the customer's behalf
Keys are never stored outside the customer's premises
why: BYOK improves customer control over key generation and lifecycle but the key lives in the provider's service. HYOK is the model where the key never leaves customer control.

q: Which TWO controls protect data at rest in a cloud database? (Choose two.)
opts: A web application firewall in front of the website
Column-level encryption of especially sensitive fields
Multi-factor authentication for console users
Transparent database or volume encryption with managed keys
TLS between the application and the database
why: Volume or database encryption and field-level encryption protect stored data. TLS protects data in transit, a firewall protects the web layer and MFA protects authentication.

q: Which TWO phases of the key lifecycle are MOST relevant to crypto-shredding? (Choose two.)
opts: Archival of keys for future decryption
Destruction of the key and all of its copies
Use of one shared key across all data sets
Distribution of keys to external partners
Generation of keys that are unique to the data being protected
why: Crypto-shredding needs per-dataset keys that can be destroyed completely. Archiving or sharing keys defeats the guarantee.

q: Hashing is a reversible process that lets the original data be recovered with the right key.
opts: True
False
why: Hashing is one-way; encryption is the reversible operation.

q: A digital signature provides integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation.
opts: True
False
why: Signing a hash with the sender's private key lets anyone verify it with the public key.

q: TLS protects data at rest in a cloud storage service.
opts: True
False
why: TLS protects data in transit; storage encryption protects data at rest.

q: Rotating keys regularly limits how much data is exposed if one key is compromised.
opts: True
False
why: Rotation shortens key lifetime and reduces the data protected by any single key.

q: Tokenization is suitable for protecting data inside a vault-backed system where real values must be retrievable by authorized services.
opts: True
False
why: The vault maps tokens back to real values for authorized use, while other systems never see the real data.

q: Under HYOK the cloud provider can still decrypt data using keys held in its own key management service.
opts: True
False
why: In HYOK the keys remain outside the provider's control, so the provider cannot decrypt.

q: A team stores training images for a model in a volume attached to a virtual machine and in an object bucket, and archives older sets to a cold tier. Which pairing of storage type and primary exposure is MOST accurate?
opts: Attached volume: unlimited public exposure through bucket policy
Object bucket: loss of all data when the instance restarts
Cold archive tier: high exposure to latency spikes during live queries
Object bucket: public access through misconfigured permissions
why: Object stores are accessed through APIs and policies, so permission mistakes are the classic exposure. Archive tiers trade retrieval speed for cost, volumes have no bucket policy and object data survives instance restarts, unlike ephemeral storage.

q: A data protection team must find where regulated records sit across hundreds of cloud accounts, including spreadsheets, a document database and application logs in JSON. Which approach is MOST suitable?
opts: Rely only on column names and table descriptions in the relational database to find sensitive data
Scan only the file shares because logs never hold personal data
Use discovery that combines schema scans, content inspection and parsing of semi-structured formats
Ask each team to email a list of what it believes it stores and take those lists as complete
why: Different data types need different techniques, and continuous automated discovery covers the estate. Column names miss content, self-reporting is incomplete and logs often contain personal data.

q: A hospital's data map shows a patient portal copying records to an analytics bucket in another country. The privacy officer wants to know the lawful basis and retention for that flow. Which artifact BEST supports this?
opts: A network diagram that shows IP address ranges and firewall rules for every environment
A data map recording sources, owners, purposes, locations and legal basis for each element
A list of users who hold administrator rights across the environments that process the data
The provider's physical data center audit report, which describes facilities rather than data flows
why: Data mapping ties each element to its purpose, location and legal basis. Network diagrams, facility reports and administrator lists do not answer lawful basis or retention.

q: A company wants every document labeled Confidential to be encrypted automatically and to carry restrictions on external sharing and copying, wherever the file is later stored. Which approach achieves this?
opts: A perimeter firewall rule that blocks any file whose name contains the word Confidential
Static masking of Confidential files before they are written to cloud storage
Classification labels that automatically apply rights management protection to the file
Folder permissions that the file server administrator sets once for each department
why: A label that triggers rights management attaches encryption and usage restrictions to the file itself, so the protection follows it. Name-based firewall rules and folder permissions stay behind when the file moves, and masking alters the content rather than controlling its use.

q: A company discovers that revoking an IRM license for a contractor did not stop the contractor from opening a copy previously downloaded to a laptop that stays offline. Which limitation does this illustrate?
opts: IRM cannot protect files stored in cloud storage because the policy server must sit in the same network
IRM works only on files smaller than a megabyte, so large documents need a different control
Revocation takes effect only when the client next checks with the policy server
IRM licenses can never be revoked once they have been issued to a recipient's device
why: Offline copies can remain usable until the agent contacts the policy server, so use short license lifetimes for sensitive material. IRM does protect cloud-stored files and licenses can be revoked.

q: A records manager moves seven-year financial archives to a cold tier encrypted with a key that is rotated and the old versions destroyed after one year. Five years later the archives cannot be opened. What went wrong?
opts: Cold tier storage cannot hold encrypted data, so the files were silently damaged in the move
The files were too old for any cloud service to read, since formats expire after about five years
The key lifecycle was not aligned with the retention period of the data it protects
Encryption should never be used for archives, because encrypted files cannot be preserved for years
why: Archive keys must survive as long as the data; destroying old key versions effectively deleted the archive. Encrypted archives are normal, and age alone does not make files unreadable.

q: An investigation requires proof that a privileged user in a SaaS tool exported a customer list on a specific date from an unfamiliar country. Which log attributes matter MOST?
opts: Only the name of the application server that wrote the log entry and the log file size
Unique identity, action, synchronized timestamp and source IP address with geolocation
The color theme and display language configured on the user's account profile
The total number of log lines written per day and the average line length
why: Accountability needs who, what, when and where, with reliable time. Server names alone, cosmetic settings and counts do not attribute an action.

q: A company wants a signed contract approval to be undeniable later. Which combination BEST provides non-repudiation?
opts: A digital signature using a private key only the signer controls, plus a trusted timestamp
A shared team account and a free-text comment field recording who agreed to the change
A hash of the document, stored in the same folder and readable by every editor
An email that states the approver's name, kept in the approver's own mailbox
why: Signatures from a private key held solely by the signer with a trusted time prove origin and integrity and resist denial. Shared accounts, an unsigned hash next to the file or a plain email can all be disputed.

q: A data science team fine-tunes a language model on customer support emails, and testing shows the model sometimes reproduces customer phone numbers in answers. Which action addresses the root cause MOST directly?
opts: Move the model to a different region so that the records are no longer near their source
Encrypt the training emails in transit only, and then use them unchanged for fine-tuning
Increase the model's response length limit so users receive fuller and more varied answers
Redact or minimize personal data in the training set before fine-tuning and test for memorization
why: Memorization of personal data comes from what was trained on, so minimization, redaction and extraction testing are the controls. Response length, region and in-transit encryption do not stop leakage from weights.

q: A research group downloads a pre-trained model file from a public registry and loads it directly into a production training pipeline with broad cloud permissions. Which risk is MOST significant?
opts: The model's accuracy will decrease automatically over time, so it must be retrained each month
The model will be unable to use any graphics processors, which makes it too slow to run safely
The registry will charge a fee for each download
The model file may contain malicious code executed on load, so it should be scanned and verified first
why: Model artifacts can embed executable code through unsafe serialization and arrive from untrusted sources; verification, scanning and sandboxed loading mitigate it. The other statements are unrelated to the security risk.

q: A legal team places a hold on mailbox data in a SaaS platform whose retention policy deletes items after 90 days. What is the MOST important step to make the hold effective?
opts: Tell custodians to stop using email until the matter closes, relying on them to keep their messages
Apply a retention lock or hold that overrides the automatic deletion rule for the relevant custodians
Wait for the deletion job to run, then restore the items from backup if anyone asks for them
Export the mailboxes to local drives and turn off logging
why: A hold must suspend automatic deletion at the platform. Local exports without governance, asking users to stop work and relying on restores risk spoliation.

q: Which TWO statements about media sanitization in a cloud context are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Console deletion always proves that every replica was erased
Customers can physically destroy the provider's disks on request
Clear, purge and destroy all require physical access to media
Cryptographic erase is a purge-level technique when strong encryption and key destruction are applied
Overwriting alone gives weak assurance on virtualized and solid-state storage
why: NIST SP 800-88 treats cryptographic erase as a purge technique, while overwriting cannot be verified across replicas and wear-leveled flash. Customers cannot destroy provider hardware, and logical deletion is not proof.

q: Which TWO controls MOST directly mitigate the threat of ransomware deleting versions and backups in cloud storage? (Choose two.)
opts: Disabling object versioning to save cost
Public read access on backup buckets
Immutable object lock or retention on backup data
A single administrator account shared by production and backup
Separate credentials and accounts for the backup repository
why: Immutability and credential separation keep attackers from erasing recovery points. Public access, shared admin credentials and no versioning make loss easier.

q: Which THREE are data rights or provisioning concepts in information rights management? (Choose three.)
opts: Binding rights to users or groups through issued certificates
Permissions such as view, print, copy and forward
Replacing the document with random tokens
Expiration dates attached to a license
Increasing the file's compression ratio
why: IRM defines what recipients may do, when rights expire and how they are issued to identities. Compression and tokenization are unrelated mechanisms.

q: Data mapping and data classification are the same activity and one can replace the other.
opts: True
False
why: Mapping records where data is, who owns it and how it flows; classification rates its sensitivity. Both are needed.

q: Raw device mapping bypasses the hypervisor's file-system abstraction, so data left on reallocated raw devices is a remanence risk.
opts: True
False
why: Raw storage gives direct device access, which is why sanitization and encryption matter before the device is reused.

q: A digital signature alone provides confidentiality for the signed document.
opts: True
False
why: Signatures give integrity, authentication and non-repudiation; confidentiality requires encryption.

q: Personal data used to train a model is exempt from privacy law once it has been absorbed into the model weights.
opts: True
False
why: Models can memorize and disclose training data, and privacy duties follow personal data through the training process.

q: Archive keys should be kept for as long as the archived data must remain readable.
opts: True
False
why: Destroying the key before retention ends makes the archive unreadable, which can breach retention duties.

q: Dynamic data masking permanently alters the stored data so the original values cannot be recovered.
opts: True
False
why: Dynamic masking changes only what a query returns by role; the stored values remain. Static masking produces an altered copy.

q: A provider stores archive objects as erasure-coded fragments spread across several regions so that any subset of fragments can rebuild the object. What is the MOST important consideration for a customer with residency rules?
opts: Dispersion removes the need for encryption because no single site holds a complete and usable copy of the object
Dispersion guarantees that the object stays inside one country because fragments are small
Dispersion makes deletion instant because every fragment expires automatically at exactly the same moment everywhere
Dispersion aids availability and limits single-site exposure, but fragment locations may breach residency rules
why: Splitting data improves resilience and reduces what any one location reveals, yet fragments in other regions can still conflict with residency requirements. It does not replace encryption or guarantee jurisdiction.

q: A team enabled management-plane audit logging for its cloud account, but an investigation cannot show who downloaded specific objects from a storage bucket. What was missing?
opts: Multi-factor authentication on the cloud console
A second copy of the audit log stored in another region
A longer retention period for the management-plane audit log
Object-level data event logging for the storage service
why: Management-plane logs record control actions such as creating buckets or changing policies, while reads and writes of individual objects are data events that usually have to be enabled separately. Retention, extra copies and console MFA do not create events that were never recorded.

q: A company builds an internal assistant that answers employee questions from a vector index of all its documents, including HR files and board papers. Which control BEST ensures that each employee only receives content they are already entitled to see?
opts: Encrypt the vector index at rest with a customer-managed key and leave retrieval open to the assistant
Tell the model in its system prompt never to reveal restricted documents to unauthorized users
Enforce the source documents' access permissions at retrieval time by filtering results for the signed-in user
Limit the chat interface to the corporate network so that only employees can reach it
why: Filtering at retrieval keeps restricted content out of the model's context in the first place. Encryption at rest does not decide who may read results, a prompt instruction can be bypassed by injection, and network location does not tell one employee from another.

q: Spreading erasure-coded fragments of data across regions can conflict with data residency requirements even though no single region holds the whole object.
opts: True
False
why: Residency rules concern where personal or regulated data is stored or processed, so fragment placement still has to be approved.

q: A cloud provider hosts multiple tenants on shared hosts. Which attack is MOST directly aimed at breaking tenant isolation?
opts: Cross-site scripting against a tenant's website
Brute-force guessing of a customer's console password
Virtual machine escape to the hypervisor
Phishing a customer's help desk
why: A VM escape defeats the isolation boundary between guests on the same host. The other attacks target customer authentication, application code or social engineering, not the multi-tenant boundary.

q: A company runs a regulated workload that must not share physical hosts with other tenants. Which option BEST meets this requirement?
opts: Dedicated hosts or single-tenant instances
Spreading instances across several availability zones
Larger virtual machine sizes on shared hosts
Enabling stricter security group rules
why: Dedicated hosts remove co-tenancy at the physical level. Larger sizes still share hardware, zones address availability and security groups filter traffic.

q: A team deploys a container image containing a known critical vulnerability to production because the pipeline has no gate. What control would have PREVENTED this?
opts: Image scanning with an admission policy that blocks vulnerable images
Enabling debug logging inside the container
Adding a bastion host in front of the cluster
Running the containers with a higher CPU quota
why: Scanning and enforcing policy at admission stops vulnerable images before they run. Quotas, bastion hosts and logging do not assess image content.

q: An engineer needs to reduce lateral movement between application tiers inside one virtual network after an incident. What is the MOST effective design change?
opts: Relying on the perimeter firewall to detect internal movement
Micro-segmentation with deny-by-default rules between workloads
Opening all ports between tiers to simplify troubleshooting during the incident
Moving all tiers into a single flat subnet for simplicity
why: Segmentation limits what a compromised host can reach. A flat network and open ports increase movement, and a perimeter device cannot see east-west traffic it never receives.

q: A serverless function that resizes images was given an access role allowing it to read every storage bucket in the account. What is the MOST appropriate action?
opts: Increase the function timeout to reduce errors
Keep the existing role but add detailed logging and alerts for all function invocations and errors
Move the function to a larger memory configuration
Replace the role with least-privilege permissions for the one bucket and actions needed
why: Over-privileged execution roles are the main serverless risk; fix by least privilege. Logging detects but does not reduce blast radius and timeouts or memory are unrelated.

q: Remote contractors need access to one internal web application only. Which approach BEST follows zero trust principles?
opts: A full-tunnel VPN placing contractors on the corporate network
Sharing a common account protected by a long password
Zero trust network access granting per-application sessions after verifying user and device
Whitelisting the contractors' home IP addresses permanently on the application firewall
why: ZTNA grants access to one application per verified session. A VPN gives broad network reach, a shared account destroys accountability and static IP addresses are unreliable and over-broad.

q: Which statement about security groups and network ACLs in a virtual private cloud is MOST accurate?
opts: Both are stateless and applied only to internet gateways
Security groups are stateful and instance-level; network ACLs are stateless and subnet-level
Network ACLs are stateful and attached to instances, while security groups are stateless and apply at subnet boundaries
Both are stateful and applied only at the instance level
why: Security groups track connections so return traffic is allowed automatically; ACLs evaluate each packet independently and need rules for both directions.

q: An organization finds that identical servers have drifted apart through manual hotfixes, making incidents hard to investigate. Which approach BEST addresses the root cause?
opts: Increasing the retention of server logs
Granting all engineers administrator access to fix problems faster
Turning off automatic updates for all hosts
Immutable infrastructure built from versioned images and templates
why: Replacing rather than modifying servers removes drift and provides known-good state. Broad admin rights make drift worse, logs do not prevent it and disabling updates adds vulnerability.

q: A dedicated private link connects an on-premises network to a cloud provider. The data classification requires confidentiality in transit. Which statement is MOST accurate?
opts: Traffic on private links can be read by any other tenant
Private links encrypt all traffic automatically at line rate with provider-managed keys
Private links remove the need for any access control
The link is private, but encryption must still be configured to meet the requirement
why: Private does not mean encrypted; layer encryption on top when required. Other tenants cannot read the traffic, but access controls are still needed.

q: A security team reviews an infrastructure-as-code pipeline. Which control is MOST valuable for preventing misconfigured resources from reaching production?
opts: Longer log retention for the deployment tool
A larger approval chain for budget changes
Manual review of resources by an engineer after they have been created
Automated policy-as-code scanning of templates before deployment
why: Pre-deployment scanning catches misconfiguration at low cost and is repeatable. After-the-fact review lets exposure occur first, and log retention or budget approval do not check security settings.

q: An attacker obtains the credentials of a cloud administrator who has no multi-factor authentication. Why is this scenario especially severe?
opts: The attacker can physically access the provider's data center
The attacker gains direct control of the provider's hypervisors and host firmware
The management plane lets the attacker create, change and delete resources
The attacker can read other customers' data directly
why: Management-plane access grants control over the customer's whole environment, which is why strong authentication is essential. Physical access, other tenants' data and hypervisor control are provider-side and not granted by customer credentials.

q: A customer asks how to confirm a provider's data center has redundant power and cooling since it cannot visit. What is the MOST appropriate source of evidence?
opts: A network scan of the provider's public addresses
Independent audit reports and certifications covering the facility
A marketing page describing the provider's data centers
The provider's verbal assurance given by a senior executive during a sales call
why: Independent reports are the dependable evidence. Marketing and verbal claims are unverified and scanning the provider's addresses is unauthorized and does not assess facilities.

q: Which TWO measures best reduce the risk of an exposed Kubernetes control plane? (Choose two.)
opts: Run all workloads with cluster-administrator permissions
Apply least-privilege role-based access control to users and service accounts
Restrict API server access to private networks and authenticated users
Disable audit logging to improve performance
Expose the dashboard publicly for convenience
why: Network restriction and least privilege shrink exposure and blast radius. The other options are common causes of cluster compromise.

q: Which TWO are typical security concerns specific to container platforms? (Choose two.)
opts: Shared host kernel across containers
Guest operating systems that need separate licenses per container
Vulnerable or untrusted base images
Hypervisor firmware updates on the customer side
why: Containers share a kernel and inherit risk from images. They do not carry their own guest operating systems, and hypervisor firmware is the provider's concern.

q: Which THREE actions help protect the cloud management plane? (Choose three.)
opts: Disable alerts on console sign-ins from new locations
Share one root account among administrators
Use just-in-time privileged access with approval
Send management API activity to a protected audit log
Require multi-factor authentication for all privileged users
why: Strong authentication, time-bound privilege and tamper-resistant logging reduce risk and support investigation. Shared root accounts remove accountability and disabled alerts blind the team.

q: Containers provide stronger isolation than virtual machines because they carry fewer components.
opts: True
False
why: Containers share the host kernel, so their isolation boundary is weaker than a VM's hypervisor-enforced boundary.

q: In serverless, the customer is responsible for patching the underlying operating system of the function host.
opts: True
False
why: The provider manages the runtime host; the customer secures code, dependencies, permissions and configuration.

q: Network access control lists are stateless, so rules must allow both inbound and the matching outbound traffic.
opts: True
False
why: ACLs evaluate each packet independently, unlike stateful security groups.

q: A Type 2 hypervisor is the usual foundation of public cloud platforms.
opts: True
False
why: Public clouds run Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors for performance and a smaller attack surface.

q: A cloud access role that grants a function broad read access across the account is acceptable if the function code is trusted.
opts: True
False
why: Least privilege limits the damage from bugs, vulnerable dependencies or injection even in trusted code.

q: A BIA shows an order system can be offline for at most two hours and can lose at most ten minutes of transactions. Which pair of objectives does this describe?
opts: RTO of two hours and RPO of ten minutes
RTO of ten minutes and RPO of two hours
Maximum tolerable downtime of ten minutes with an RPO of two hours
RTO and RPO both of two hours
why: RTO measures time to restore service and RPO measures tolerable data loss in time. The other pairings reverse or conflate them.

q: A company has an RTO of four hours and an RPO of 24 hours for an internal reporting tool and wants the lowest-cost recovery option. Which strategy fits?
opts: Warm standby with continuous replication
Backup and restore with nightly backups
Active-active deployment across two regions
Synchronous replication to a hot standby
why: The relaxed targets are met by daily backups and manual rebuild. The other options meet far stricter objectives at much higher cost.
